extracted.intended_audience: aspiring novelists and literary critics studying narrative method
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for novelists on when and how to use strictly dramatic (scene/action-driven) methods versus discursive/omniscient narration, including when to mix methods and how to handle background, setting, and recurring characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show motives through action (dramatic showing)
rubrics_metrics.description: The root of the matter is in their behaviour; their action fully covers their motives and sentiments — their behaviour will sufficiently express what is in their minds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid interior exposition when characters' visible and audible signs can betray motives. By clever management the author can avoid looking inside motives; make acts carry meaning so no explanatory narrator is needed. Example: Nanda's action answers the question and provides the issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use no narrator when the subject is pure action
rubrics_metrics.description: The theme being an action merely and strictly limited in scope, it requires no narrator; the characters may set it forth on their own account, and we have only to look on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer a strictly dramatic method for compact stories involving a small, well-defined company and incident. If the story can 'act itself out from beginning to end' keep narration minimal or absent for immediacy and consistency (example: The Awkward Age).

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain consistency and homogeneity of method
rubrics_metrics.description: Method becomes as consistent and homogeneous as it ever may in fiction; no other manner of telling can be quite so true to itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once you choose a dominant method (dramatic or discursive), sustain it unless you have clear artistic reason to break it. Inconsistent mixing without purpose can undermine truthfulness of effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize drama's limitation in expressing background and atmosphere
rubrics_metrics.description: The dramatic scene is vivid and compact; but it is narrow, it can have no great depth, and the colour of the atmosphere can hardly tell within the space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a story's effect depends on its surround ings, time, or broad social atmosphere, supplement strict drama with authorial survey or descriptive narration; drama alone may fail to convey outlying associations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use mixed methods when background or wide survey is required
rubrics_metrics.description: Even in dealing with a subject entirely dramatic, a novelist may well find reason to keep to his old familiar mixed method — circumspice: it would appear that he does so invariably.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine pictorial/ descriptive material with dramatic scenes to give depth, context, and credibility (Balzac/Dickens examples). Only pursue pure drama 'a outrance' when the gain justifies the difficulty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider practical difficulty of strict dramatic rule
rubrics_metrics.description: To treat a subject with the rigour of Henry James is extremely difficult... a novel is more likely to fall below its proper dramatic pitch than to strain beyond it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh the craft demands: making every motive evident purely through action is hard; the omniscient narrator is often the simpler option. Choose bold strictness only when you can sustain it artistically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unnecessary omniscient-authorial intrusion
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an easy-going reliance on a narrator of some kind, a showman who ... can tell us all about it. He seems to come forward... without doing the story any particular service; sometimes he actually embarrasses it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use the narrator merely for the convenience of explaining characters' motives or supplying color the action could supply. Silence the spokesman when the issue can flower unaided in the scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use pictorial/scene-setting to supply character and energy
rubrics_metrics.description: A pictorial impression, wrought to the right pitch, will speed the work of drama — will become an effective agent in the book, instead of remaining the mere decorative introduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ background description economically to provide the reserve of vigor that drives later action (Balzac's Maison Vauquer, Dickens' populated scenes leading into climax). Let setting function as prepared character and force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy in descriptive preparatory pictures
rubrics_metrics.description: Balzac's care in creating the scene... is truly economical; it is not merely a manner of setting the stage for the drama, it is a provision of character and energy for the drama when it begins.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Descriptions should be crafted so that they directly serve the drama — deepen motive, supply pressure, make later events credible — rather than merely display fact-for-fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shed irrelevant past associations when reusing characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Of the characters in the remoter planes of the action... no more is expected than their value for the purpose of the action in the foreground... whatever more they may bring will lie idle, will contribute nothing, and may even become an embarrassment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If reusing characters from other works, avoid importing irrelevant backstory or associations that distract from the present foreground action; retain only what serves the current story's unity and truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temper unbelievable drama by grounding in descriptive truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the action is likely to seem harsh, overcharged, romantic, it is made to look less so, less hazardous and more real, by recourse to the art of the picture-maker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a plot or climax risks incredibility, use broader, familiar, and well-populated scenes to lead into and justify it (Dickens' technique) so the reader accepts the romantic or extreme action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Even subjective/meditative prose needs particularized incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: No story-teller... can use a manner as strictly subjective... Pater... the flow of his rumination is interrupted while he pauses... to make them visible; they must be given a kind of objectivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing dreamy, subjective, or retrospective narratives, include definite images or occasions (scenes 'caught in the act') to anchor the reader and give the work sufficient dramatic presence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose method based on whether setting/time are central
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the effect of the action depends upon its time and place, a novelist naturally turns to the obvious method... if the effect depends on its time and place the novelist will use descriptive method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If your story's meaning arises from a distinctive milieu or historical specificity, favor methods that clearly establish setting; strict drama may not adequately convey necessary background.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor compactness and limited cast for strictly dramatic works
rubrics_metrics.description: The situation involves no more than a small company of people, and there is no reason for them to straggle far, in space or time; the compactness of the situation is one of its special marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strictly dramatic novels work best when the incident is confined, the cast limited, and episodes closely connected; larger canvases generally call for discursive survey techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be wary of description-for-its-own-sake (over-enthusiastic detail)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are times when his inexhaustible knowledge of facts is carrying him where it will, till his only conscious purpose is to set down on paper everything that he knows... there is nothing more tiresome in Balzac than his zest... when he forgets that he is a novelist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid indulging in descriptive digressions that do not serve the present action; excessive factual display can slow the drama and distract the reader even if it later enriches setting.
